<reason>An elite, genuinely clashing debate. B was often flashier: the withdrawal-period point ("a bioreactor has no metabolism"), "no carcass has a passage number," and the vacuity dilemma were the debate's sharpest hits, and B rightly exposed A's opening false dichotomy. But A won the structural question the motion actually asks. A's reading of "same basic terms" as parity in legal standing within one hazard-based framework is the more faithful reading of the text: the pre-market gate is absorbed by the motion's own condition ("once safety standards are met"), and A's HACCP/oysters-canned-ham framing showed B was mostly naming hazards, not a rival regime. Crucially, when B's Q1 demanded whether the motion has any content, A answered directly with three real violations (name bans, warning labels, procurement exclusion) that map onto actual Italy/US-state policies — B never re-engaged that answer, leaving its "contentless motion" attack undercut. B's closing leaned on A's silence about cell-line authentication, but that was a standing requirement B only crystallized in its own prior speech and A had covered generically. B's "trap collapses on their own examples" jab in A4.2 was chronologically premature (B answered Q1 fully in B4.1), a real execution mark-down, and both sides had one clipped turn, roughly canceling. Net: B won several exchanges but never destabilized A's frame; A made the debate easier to decide as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B's vacuity trap (B3.1/B4.6: name one requirement short of a ban that violates the motion, or concede it means nothing) met by A4.1's concrete triad — forbidding the word "chicken," warning-style labels, procurement exclusion — which gave "same basic terms" real content against live policies; B never squarely answered it afterward. The sharpest single hit, though, was B2.5's point that conventional residue testing presumes a metabolizing animal's withdrawal period while a bioreactor has none.</best_rebuttal>
